chunks.title: Aqueous in & out
chunks.tldr: Made by the ciliary epithelium (pars plicata). Leaves via trabecular meshwork (90%) or uveoscleral (10%). Most resistance sits in the juxtacanalicular meshwork.
points: Production: ultrafiltration from capillaries + active secretion by the 2-layer ciliary epithelium → water follows.
Beta-2 receptors ↑ production. Alpha-2 receptors ↓ production. Carbonic anhydrase is key.
Trabecular meshwork, inside → out: uveal (big holes) → corneoscleral (thickest) → juxtacanalicular/cribriform (most resistance).
Schlemm canal: inner wall has giant vacuoles/pores → collector channels → episcleral veins.
Trabecular route (90%): pressure-dependent. Uveoscleral (10%): across the ciliary body face into the suprachoroidal space. Some via the iris.
IOP = production vs outflow (resistance + episcleral venous pressure).
Normal: mean 16 mmHg, range 11–21. IOP is highest in the morning. Glaucoma eyes swing more → note the time.
chunks.hook: Meshwork layers inside-out: U-C-J ('U C Jammed' = juxtacanalicular jams it).

cards.q: Which part of the trabecular meshwork gives most outflow resistance?
Which receptors increase aqueous production?

chunks.title: Ocular hypertension (OHT) & OHTS
chunks.tldr: OHT = IOP >21, open angle, no damage. ~1 in 10 convert over 10 years. OHTS risk factors: high IOP, older age, thin CCT (<555), big C/D, high PSD.
points: 4–7% of over-40s. Upper normal in over-70s ≈ 23 mmHg.
OHTS: treatment (20% IOP drop) cut 5-year conversion from 9.5% → 4.4%.
Significant risks (multivariate): IOP, age, CCT, C/D ratio, PSD.
Thin cornea (<555 µm) = higher risk; thick (>588) = lower.
Univariate only: African ethnicity, male, heart disease.
Not significant in OHTS: myopia, diabetes, family history (surprisingly).
Gene: TMCO1 variant linked to conversion.
Use risk calculators. Most treat IOP ≥30 (>40% 5-year risk). Consider age/life expectancy. OHT also ↑ retinal vein occlusion risk.
Pre-perimetric glaucoma: disc/RNFL damage but fields still normal.
chunks.hook: OHTS 5: Pressure, Pachymetry, Peeking cup, PSD, Pension age.

cards.q: OHTS: what CCT value increased conversion risk?
5-year conversion in untreated vs treated OHTS?

chunks.title: Glaucoma overview & POAG risk factors
chunks.tldr: Glaucoma = progressive optic neuropathy with cupping + RNFL loss + field loss. IOP is the only thing we can change. POAG risks: IOP, age, black ethnicity, family history, myopia.
points: 2–3% of over-40s, half undiagnosed. 2nd leading cause of blindness. POAG commonest in whites/blacks; angle closure up to half worldwide (Asians).
EMGT untreated loss: HTG −1.31 dB/yr, NTG −0.36, PXF −3.13 (fastest).
POAG: adult, open angle, no secondary cause. Over 70: ~6% white, 16% black, 3% Asian.

Risks: IOP (and asymmetry ≥4 mmHg), age, black race (4×, earlier, harder), family history (siblings 4×, children 2×), myopia, anti-VEGF injections, long-term OCP, vascular disease, low perfusion pressure, large discs, translaminar pressure gradient.
Diabetes: no proven risk in longitudinal studies.
Genes: MYOC (myocilin) and OPTN (optineurin). Glaucoma before 35 → MYOC chance up to 33%.
Damage: ganglion cell apoptosis. Mechanical (lamina cribrosa) ± ischaemic.
Screen: high-risk groups (older, family history, African). Tonometry alone isn't enough: add discs and fields.
chunks.hook: Glaucoma = slow thief of sight. IOP is the one lock we can fit.

cards.q: Which glaucoma type progressed fastest untreated in EMGT?
Gene most associated with juvenile-onset POAG?

chunks.title: POAG history & exam
chunks.tldr: Usually no symptoms. Ask about steroids, asthma/heart block (no beta-blockers), sulfa allergy (no acetazolamide). Do tonometry before pachymetry, gonioscopy before dilating.
points: History: refraction (myopia → POAG, hyperopia → angle closure), trauma, uveitis, surgery (incl. LASIK → falsely low IOP), family history.
Medical: asthma, COPD, heart failure/block (beta-blocker contraindications), head injury/stroke (other causes of field loss), migraine/Raynaud, OCP.
Drugs: steroids (creams, inhalers too), oral beta-blockers (lower IOP), sulfonamide allergy → avoid acetazolamide.
Exam: VA (usually fine), RAPD (new RAPD = progression), colour if other neuropathy suspected.
Slit lamp: look for PXF, pigment dispersion (secondary causes).
Tonometry (note time) → pachymetry → gonioscopy → dilate (if angle safe) → disc exam (red-free light for RNFL).
chunks.hook: Before any drop: Lungs, Heart, Sulfa.

cards.q: Allergy that contraindicates acetazolamide?
Why do gonioscopy before dilating?
cards.a: To make sure the angle isn't critically narrow (risk of angle closure).

chunks.title: The normal disc: ISNT & disc size
chunks.tldr: Rim thickness order: I > S > N > T. Big disc = big cup (can be normal). Any cup in a small disc is suspicious. C/D asymmetry ≥0.2 = suspicious.
points: Neuroretinal rim (NRR) = pink tissue between cup and disc edge.
ISNT rule: Inferior thickest, then Superior, Nasal, Temporal. Sensitive (81%) but not specific (32%).
Use the vertical C/D ratio. Only 2% have C/D >0.7.
Asymmetry ≥0.2 = suspicious (but check the discs are the same size).
Disc size: normal vertical ~1.5–1.7 mm (whites), largest in Africans. Big discs may be more vulnerable (NTG).
Measure with a slit beam + fundus lens. Correction factors: Volk 60D ×0.88–1.0, 78D ×1.1, 90D ×1.3, 3-mirror ×1.27.
chunks.hook: ISNT = 'I See Nerve Tissue' (inferior thickest).

cards.q: ISNT rule order?
cards.a: Inferior ≥ Superior ≥ Nasal ≥ Temporal rim thickness.

cards.q: Correction factor for a Volk 90D lens when measuring disc size?

chunks.title: Glaucomatous disc signs
chunks.tldr: Look for: enlarging cup, notching, disc haemorrhage, baring of vessels, bayoneting, nasal rim loss, laminar dots, beta-zone PPA, RNFL wedge defects.
points: A documented increase in cup size is always significant.

4 disc types: focal ischaemic (notch, early fixation threat), myopic glaucomatous (tilted, temporal crescent, young men), sclerotic (shallow saucer cup, older, vascular disease), concentric enlargement (even rim loss, high IOP).
Disc haemorrhage: usually inferotemporal, risk for progression, more in NTG (but 3 of 4 people with one don't have glaucoma).
Baring of circumlinear vessels: gap between vessel and rim (early).
Bayoneting: vessel kinks twice at the rim edge.
Collateral vessels, nasal rim loss (moderate–advanced), laminar dot sign, 'sharpened rim'.
Peripapillary atrophy: alpha (outer, RPE changes) and beta (inner, chorioretinal atrophy), beta = progression risk, points to the field defect side.
RNFL: arcuate fibres at the superotemporal/inferotemporal poles are most vulnerable; papillomacular bundle most resistant. Fibres don't cross the horizontal raphe.
RNFL defects come before disc and field changes. Wedge or diffuse. See with red-free light or OCT.
chunks.hook: Haemorrhage at the disc = warning flare. Look with magnification.

cards.q: Which RNFL fibres are most resistant to glaucoma?
Which PPA zone is linked to glaucoma progression?
Disc haemorrhages are especially common in which glaucoma?

chunks.title: Imaging: OCT, UBM & friends
chunks.tldr: OCT RNFL is great for suspects and early–moderate glaucoma, but hits a 'floor' (~45–50 µm) in advanced disease → use macular GCC. UBM sees behind the iris.
points: Imaging supplements clinical exam and fields, never replaces them.
Pachymetry: essential.
Stereo disc photos: historical gold standard.
UBM: high-frequency ultrasound. Best for ciliary body/lens behind the iris (plateau iris, angle closure).
AS-OCT: iris–angle relationship (thick iris, anterior insertion, iris roll). Non-contact.
AC depth: OCT, ultrasound, IOLMaster.
OCT RNFL: circle scan around the disc vs normative database (~90% sensitivity/specificity). Don't compare between machines. ~4 µm test–retest variability.
Floor effect: RNFL stops thinning at ~45–50 µm → limited in advanced disease.
Ganglion cell complex (macula: RNFL + GCL + IPL): as good as RNFL, useful when the disc is hard to read.
Trend-based progression analysis on serial scans.
Also: confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (HRT), scanning laser polarimetry (GDx).
chunks.hook: OCT is a great early warning system, but goes quiet at the floor.

cards.q: What is the OCT 'floor effect'?
cards.a: RNFL thickness stops falling (~45–50 µm) despite ongoing damage in advanced glaucoma.

cards.q: Main advantage of UBM over AS-OCT?
cards.a: It images structures behind the iris (ciliary body, lens).

chunks.title: Glaucoma visual fields
chunks.tldr: Field loss follows nerve fibres: paracentral → nasal step → arcuate → ring → central/temporal island. Stage by MD: early <−6, moderate −6 to −12, severe >−12 dB.
points: SAP is insensitive early (FDT/SWAP pick up earlier).
Early: more variability, slight asymmetry between eyes.
Paracentral depressions (often superonasal; common in NTG).
Nasal step: respects the horizontal midline (raphe). Temporal wedge less common.
Arcuate defects 10–20° from fixation, from the blind spot curving around.
Ring scotoma (advanced) → central + temporal island (end-stage; use 10-2).
Untreated ~1 dB/year average MD loss.
Hodapp–Parrish–Anderson minimal criteria (any one, on 2 consecutive fields): GHT outside normal limits; cluster of ≥3 non-edge points at p<5% with one at p<1%; CPSD/PSD p<5%.
Any 0 dB point in the central 5° = severe.
chunks.hook: Field loss hugs the horizontal line (the nerve fibre raphe).

cards.q: Mean deviation range for moderate glaucomatous loss?
Why does a nasal step respect the horizontal midline?
cards.a: Nerve fibres don't cross the horizontal raphe.

chunks.title: Managing POAG: target pressure
chunks.tldr: Set a target IOP (start: <18 mmHg, AGIS). Every 1 mmHg lower = 10% less progression (EMGT). Start with one drug (PGA or beta-blocker) or SLT. Poor adherence in ≥25%.
points: Goal: keep useful vision for the patient's lifetime. Only proven method: lower IOP. High mean IOP and big fluctuations both predict progression.
Teach drop technique + punctal occlusion / eye closure for 3 minutes. Explain side effects.
Target depends on: damage (C/D, MD), IOP level, CCT, speed of progression, age/health.
AGIS: IOP always <18 → little progression.
EMGT: each 1 mmHg drop → ~10% less risk.
Progressing at target → lower the target. Still progressing → surgery.
Start: lowest dose, fewest side effects, usually a prostaglandin or beta-blocker. Review at 4–8 weeks.
No response → swap. Partial → add/combine. 2 drops → wait 5 min between.
Fields every 6–12 months, gonioscopy yearly (angles narrow with age), disc each visit (haemorrhages).
Failure causes: target too high, non-adherence, IOP swings, or another diagnosis (compressive lesion).
SLT: as good as one drop → first-line option. Trabeculectomy, tubes, non-penetrating, MIGS. Phaco alone lowers IOP ~15%.
Lifetime bilateral blindness historically 5–10%.
chunks.hook: Every 1 mmHg counts (10%). Aim below 18.

cards.q: Which trial suggested keeping IOP always below 18 mmHg?
EMGT: risk reduction per 1 mmHg IOP decrease?

chunks.title: Normal-tension glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Glaucoma with IOP ≤21. Think: thin CCT, nocturnal BP dips, migraine/Raynaud, Japanese, disc haemorrhages. Exclude a brain lesion if colour/field/pallor don't fit.
points: 30–65% of open-angle glaucoma may have normal IOP at first.

Risks: older, women?, Japanese, family history, OPTN, low CCT, vasospasm (migraine, Raynaud), nocturnal hypotension (>20% dip, esp. evening antihypertensives), sleep apnoea, low perfusion pressure, myopia, thyroid.

Exclude: angle closure (dark-room gonio), thin cornea/LASIK, POAG with IOP spikes (phasing), past steroids/uveitis/trauma, oral beta-blockers, burnt-out pigmentary glaucoma, myopic/drusen RNFL loss, disc pit/coloboma, compressive lesion, old AION (GCA!), past shock/blood loss.
Discs: often larger, more disc haemorrhages, acquired pits, focal RNFL defects, PPA.
Fields: closer to fixation, deeper, steeper.
Neuroimage if: VA loss out of proportion, colour loss, field not matching RNFL, rim pallor, rapid progression.
Bloods: B12, folate, FBC, ESR/CRP, syphilis/Lyme, ACE, protein electrophoresis. 24-h BP. Carotid Doppler.
~50% don't progress over 5–7 years → prove progression before treating (unless advanced).
Treat: prostaglandin first. Brimonidine (maybe neuroprotective). Avoid bedtime beta-blockers (BP dip); betaxolol if needed. SLT. Trab with antimetabolite.
Also: fix nocturnal hypotension, sleep head-up (IOP ~20% lower), avoid headstands.
chunks.hook: NTG? Ask: Is the brain or blood pressure the real culprit?

cards.q: Why avoid bedtime topical beta-blockers in NTG?
cards.a: They can worsen nocturnal systemic hypotension (reduced optic nerve perfusion).

cards.q: Name 3 indications for neuroimaging in suspected NTG.
cards.a: VA loss out of proportion, colour vision loss, field not matching RNFL, rim pallor, rapid progression.

chunks.title: Grading the angle (Shaffer & van Herick)
chunks.tldr: Shaffer 4 (35–45°, wide) → 3 (scleral spur seen) → 2 (TM seen, ~20°) → 1 (only Schwalbe, ~10°) → slit → 0 (closed). Van Herick ≤¼ → do gonioscopy.
points: Angle closure = iris touching the trabecular meshwork (iridotrabecular contact, ITC).
PACG = up to half of glaucoma worldwide, common in Asia, more blinding than POAG.
Angle is usually narrowest superiorly.
Shaffer: 4 = myopes/pseudophakes, ciliary body visible. 3 = scleral spur visible. 2 = TM but not spur. 1 = Schwalbe ± top of TM. Slit = nothing visible but no contact. 0 = closed.
Indentation tells appositional from synechial closure.
Spaeth (detailed). Scheie: higher Roman numeral = narrower (opposite!).
Van Herick: thin slit at 60°, compare peripheral AC depth to corneal thickness. ≥1 = grade 4. ¼–½ = 3. ¼ = 2 (gonioscope). <¼ = 1 (dangerous). Can miss plateau iris.
chunks.hook: Shaffer: bigger number = bigger angle. Scheie is the rebel (bigger = narrower).

cards.q: Shaffer grade where TM is seen but not the scleral spur?
Van Herick grade needing gonioscopy?
cards.a: Grade 2 (peripheral AC = ¼ corneal thickness) or less.

chunks.title: PACS → PAC → PACG
chunks.tldr: PACS = ITC ≥3 quadrants only. PAC = + raised IOP or PAS, nerve OK. PACG = + glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
points: Primary angle closure suspect (PACS): shallow AC, 'eclipse sign' (shadow on the nasal iris from temporal light), ITC in ≥3 quadrants (or 2 + pigment smudging), normal IOP, disc and field, no PAS.
ZAP study: untreated PACS → only ~8 per 1000 eye-years progress (4.2 with laser PI). Low risk.
Primary angle closure (PAC): ≥3 quadrants ITC + raised IOP and/or PAS. Disc and field normal. (Ischaemic PAC = signs of a past attack, e.g. glaukomflecken.)
PACG: ITC + glaucomatous optic neuropathy. After an acute attack the nerve may be pale rather than cupped.
chunks.hook: Suspect → Closure (pressure/PAS) → Glaucoma (nerve damage).

cards.q: Difference between PAC and PACG?
cards.a: PACG has glaucomatous optic neuropathy; PAC does not.

cards.q: What did the ZAP trial show?
cards.a: PACS has a low risk of progression; laser PI roughly halves it.

chunks.title: Mechanisms: pupil block, plateau iris, lens
chunks.tldr: Pupil block → iris bows forward → laser PI fixes it. Plateau iris → flat iris, ciliary processes push the periphery forward → closes despite a patent PI ('double hump' on indentation).
points: Relative pupillary block: aqueous can't get through the pupil → posterior pressure → iris bombé. Peripheral iridotomy equalises pressure. Won't work if lots of PAS or TM damage.
Lens vault: how much lens sits in front of the angle → big vault = angle closure risk.
Non-pupillary block: common in Asians, deeper AC, younger. Thick peripheral iris roll, anterior iris insertion.
Plateau iris configuration: flat central iris, near-normal central AC, very narrow recess, anteriorly rotated ciliary processes. Double hump sign on indentation gonio. Confirm with UBM.
Plateau iris syndrome: angle stays closed after a patent PI (complete = high IOP; incomplete = normal IOP).
Lens-induced: intumescent lens (phacomorphic) or subluxed lens.
Retrolenticular: malignant glaucoma, posterior segment causes.
Outflow loss from: iris contact, TM damage, and PAS (extent of PAS predicts IOP control).
chunks.hook: PI fixes pupil block. PI doesn't fix plateau.

cards.q: Gonioscopic sign of plateau iris on indentation?
Best imaging to confirm plateau iris?
cards.a: Ultrasound biomicroscopy (shows anteriorly rotated ciliary processes).

chunks.title: Acute angle closure: who, triggers, signs
chunks.tldr: Older hyperopic woman, often Asian, in a dark room or after dilating drops/meds → painful red eye, haloes, vomiting, IOP 50–80, hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated oval pupil.
points: Risks: age (~62), female, Asian, family history, hyperopia (1 in 6 with ≥+1 D are PACS → gonioscope them), short axial length, nanophthalmos.

Triggers: dark room/TV, mydriatic drops, reading face-down, stress, anticholinergics/sympathomimetics (inhalers, travel patches, cold remedies), topiramate (ciliary effusion → bilateral, myopic shift).
Intermittent: blur ('smoke'), haloes ('rainbows'), headache.
Acute: VA 6/60–HM, IOP 50–80, ciliary flush, corneal oedema, shallow AC, flare, fixed mid-dilated vertically oval pupil, nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain.
Other eye: narrow angle (if not → think secondary cause).
After the attack: early low IOP (ciliary shutdown), Descemet folds. Late: spiral iris atrophy, glaukomflecken, irregular pupil, posterior synechiae, pale/cupped disc.
Most angle closure is silent (chronic 'creeping' closure, saw-tooth PAS).
chunks.hook: Haloes + headache + hazy cornea + half-dilated pupil = acute angle closure.

cards.q: Classic pupil in acute angle closure?
Anti-epileptic causing bilateral angle closure via ciliary effusion?

chunks.title: Angle closure tests & differentials
chunks.tldr: Back up gonioscopy with AS-OCT/UBM. Dark-room prone test: IOP rise ≥8 mmHg = positive. Acute high IOP differentials: phacomorphic, malignant glaucoma, NVG, Posner–Schlossman, herpetic uveitis.
points: AS-OCT / UBM / Scheimpflug: supplement gonioscopy, good for teaching patients.
AC depth, biometry (if lens surgery), B-scan if atypical.
Pharmacological dilation test: poor and risky.
Dark-room prone provocative test: face down in the dark for 1 h (awake) → IOP up ≥8 mmHg + closed angle = positive. Positive despite patent PI → plateau iris. Lens extraction abolishes it.

Differentials for sudden high IOP: swollen/subluxed lens, malignant glaucoma (recent surgery), secondary angle closure, neovascular glaucoma, hypertensive uveitis (HSV/VZV/CMV, Posner–Schlossman), scleritis.
chunks.hook: Dark room, face down, +8 = positive.

cards.q: Threshold IOP rise for a positive dark-room prone provocative test?

chunks.title: Treating acute angle closure
chunks.tldr: Lie flat → acetazolamide 500 mg (IV if IOP >50) → topical timolol + apraclonidine + steroid → pilocarpine 2% (not if IOP >40) → mannitol if stuck → bilateral laser PI once the cornea clears.
points: Supine (lens falls back).
Acetazolamide 500 mg: IV if IOP >50, oral (not slow release) if <50. Not with sulfa allergy or topiramate-induced closure.
One drop each of apraclonidine, timolol, steroid (3–5 min apart).
Pilocarpine 2% in the affected eye (repeat in 30 min), 1% in the other eye. Don't repeat if IOP >40 (ischaemic iris won't respond, can push the lens forward, toxicity).
Pain relief + antiemetic.
Resistant: corneal indentation (squint hook / goniolens), glycerol 50% drops to clear the cornea, mannitol 20% 1–2 g/kg IV or oral glycerol/isosorbide, early laser PI or iridoplasty, paracentesis.
Then: pilocarpine QID, steroid QID, timolol/apraclonidine/acetazolamide as needed.
Bilateral laser PI once cornea is clear. Repeat gonioscopy to confirm the angle is open.
Surgery options: iridectomy, lens extraction, goniosynechialysis, trab, cyclodiode.
chunks.hook: Flat, Diamox, 3 drops, Pilo, PI both eyes.

cards.q: Why not keep giving pilocarpine if IOP stays above 40 in acute angle closure?
cards.a: Iris sphincter ischaemia blocks its effect, it can shift the lens forward, and risks systemic toxicity.

cards.q: Definitive treatment after breaking an acute attack?

chunks.title: Long-term: PACS, PAC, PACG & EAGLE
chunks.tldr: PACS → laser PI only if high risk (ZAP). Still closed after PI → observe, iridoplasty, pilocarpine, or lens extraction. EAGLE: clear lens extraction beats PI for PAC with IOP >29 or PACG.
points: PACS: PI has a modest effect → offer to the highest-risk people.
ITC persists after PI: observe (most), laser iridoplasty, pilocarpine 1% BD, or phaco if there's cataract.
PAC/PACG: same, but lower threshold to do more. Medical treatment as POAG if PAS or high IOP persists.
Phaco + IOL deepens the AC and opens the angle → IOP controlled in almost all with normal pre-op IOP, ~80% with high IOP.
EAGLE trial: clear lens extraction more effective and cost-effective than PI for PAC (IOP >29) or PACG.
Trab + MMC: option, but risk of malignant glaucoma in these short eyes.
chunks.hook: EAGLE: the lens is the enemy in angle closure.

cards.q: Main conclusion of the EAGLE trial?
cards.a: Clear lens extraction is more effective and cost-effective than laser PI for PAC with IOP >29 mmHg or PACG.

chunks.title: Secondary glaucoma map
chunks.tldr: Open-angle: pre-trabecular (membrane: NVG, ICE, epithelial ingrowth), trabecular (clogged: pigment, PXF, blood, ghost cells, lens protein), post-trabecular (high episcleral venous pressure). Closed-angle: with or without pupil block.
points: Pre-trabecular: fibrovascular (neovascular), endothelial (ICE), epithelial (ingrowth) membranes.
Trabecular: pigment, red cells, ghost cells, macrophages/lens protein (phacolytic), PXF material, proteins; trabeculitis; scarring (angle recession).
Post-trabecular: CCF, Sturge–Weber, SVC obstruction.
Closed + pupil block: seclusio pupillae, subluxed lens, phacomorphic, capsular block, aphakic block, AC IOL without PI.
Closed, no pupil block: PAS from NVG/uveitis, ciliochoroidal effusion, iris/ciliary cysts or tumours, contracting retrolental tissue (PVR, ROP), malignant glaucoma.
chunks.hook: Before, In, After the meshwork.

cards.q: Give 2 post-trabecular causes of secondary glaucoma.
Which secondary glaucomas are pre-trabecular?
cards.a: Neovascular glaucoma, ICE syndrome, epithelial ingrowth.

chunks.title: Pseudoexfoliation (PXF)
chunks.tldr: Commonest secondary open-angle glaucoma. White dandruff on the lens (central disc + peripheral ring), Sampaolesi line, pupil-edge transillumination. LOXL1. High, swinging IOP → worse than POAG.
points: Older (>50; ~5% at 75–85), women, highest in Scandinavia. Systemic (skin, organs) → linked to hearing loss, heart disease.
Gene: LOXL1 (chromosome 15). High homocysteine, low folate?
15–30% have glaucoma at diagnosis; up to 60% need treatment at 5 years. Often one eye (2/3).
Signs: central disc + peripheral ring of material on the anterior capsule (clear zone from pupil rubbing), flaky edges, best seen dilated.
Iris: pupillary ruff loss, moth-eaten transillumination at the pupil edge.
Gonio: patchy pigment (inferior), Sampaolesi line, dandruff deposits. Higher angle-closure risk (loose zonules).
Cataract more common; phacodonesis, poor dilation.
IOP high and fluctuating → can rise acutely with an open angle.

Treat: drops fail more often. SLT works well (~30%) but careful energy (pigment). Phaco alone may lower IOP; surgery risky (zonules, capsule, endothelium, IOP spike, phimosis, late IOL dislocation). Review ≤6-monthly.
chunks.hook: PXF = Pretty eXcessive Fluctuation (IOP) and fragile zonules.

cards.q: Gene associated with pseudoexfoliation?
Irregular pigment line on or anterior to Schwalbe line?

chunks.title: Pigment dispersion & pigmentary glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Young myopic man. Iris bows backwards and rubs zonules → Krukenberg spindle, radial spoke transillumination, dense TM pigment band. IOP spikes after exercise.
points: ~15% of PDS develop high IOP/glaucoma by 15 years. AD in some families. Myopia = earlier, worse.
Mechanism: reverse pupil block → posterior bowing → iris pigment epithelium rubs on zonules. PI flattens the iris.
Shedding decreases with age (IOP may normalise → mistaken for NTG).
Steroid responders more common.
Signs: Krukenberg spindle (vertical pigment on endothelium), deep AC, radial mid-peripheral spoke-like transillumination, pigment on iris.
Gonio: wide open, concave iris, dense even 360° TM pigment band.
Lens: Scheie stripe / Zentmayer ring at the zonular insertion.
Posterior: lattice, higher RD risk.
Treat: limit heavy exercise if it triggers attacks. Drops as POAG (miotics help in theory but cause myopia/RD risk).
SLT: low energy, 2 quadrants (pigmented angle → spikes). Laser PI flattens the iris, reduces spikes (<40 y) but doesn't prevent glaucoma.
Trab more often needed; young myopes → hypotony/suprachoroidal haemorrhage risk.
BADI/BAIT: sudden bilateral iris depigmentation/transillumination + high IOP in women, after flu or moxifloxacin.
chunks.hook: PDS: young myopic man jogging → blurry haloes.

cards.q: Vertical pigment deposit on the corneal endothelium in PDS?
Mechanism of iris pigment release in PDS?
cards.a: Posterior iris bowing (reverse pupil block) rubbing against zonules.

chunks.title: Neovascular glaucoma (NVG)
chunks.tldr: Retinal ischaemia → VEGF → new vessels on the pupil edge → iris → angle → fibrovascular membrane closes the angle. Causes: ischaemic CRVO ('100-day glaucoma'), diabetes, ocular ischaemia. Treat: anti-VEGF + PRP + IOP control.
points: Ischaemic CRVO (35–50%): VA <6/60, RAPD, big non-perfusion → NVG ~3 months later.
Diabetes: now 10–15% (screening, PRP, anti-VEGF). Vitrectomy can trigger it (esp. if angle NV before).
Others: CRAO, ocular ischaemic syndrome, tumours, long-standing RD, chronic inflammation.
Early sign: fine vessels at the pupil margin (high magnification!). Then radial iris vessels.
Gonioscopy (undilated) in at-risk eyes: angle NV can come first.
Late: angle zips shut → very high IOP, pain, corneal oedema, hyphaema, ectropion uveae.
Treat: IOP drops (no miotics), atropine, topical steroid. Careful with acetazolamide in diabetics (kidneys).
PRP (indirect laser, cryo if hazy) + intravitreal/intracameral bevacizumab (fast relief; repeat). Small CRAO risk in OIS.
Fix RD. Cyclodiode if IOP uncontrolled. Tube or trab + MMC if vision HM or better (control NV first).
Painful blind eye: retrobulbar alcohol, enucleation.
Prognosis poor: 25–50% blind; life expectancy ~halved.
chunks.hook: CRVO + 100 days = NVG. Look at the pupil edge with high mag.

cards.q: Typical interval from ischaemic CRVO to NVG?
Earliest sign of iris neovascularisation?
cards.a: Fine new vessels at the pupillary margin.

chunks.title: Uveitic glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Mechanisms: seclusio pupillae → iris bombé, PAS, trabeculitis, debris, steroids. Acute flares often lower IOP (ciliary shutdown). Use beta-blocker first; avoid prostaglandins and miotics.
points: Common in Fuchs uveitis and JIA. Posterior uveitis rarely raises IOP.
Problems: small pupil, cloudy media, IOP swings, ciliary shutdown hides high IOP, steroid fluctuations, iris vessels mimic NVG.
With pupil block: 360° posterior synechiae (seclusio pupillae) → iris bombé → angle closure → PAS. → laser PI (+ intensive steroid) or surgical iridectomy.
Without pupil block: inflammatory debris organises → progressive PAS (deep AC, closed angle).
Open angle: trabecular clogging, protein, trabeculitis (HSV, VZV, CMV, toxo), chronic scarring, steroids.
Drugs: beta-blocker first. CAI (can be very effective), alpha-agonist. Avoid PGAs (inflammation, CMO) and miotics (synechiae). No depot steroids in responders.
Surgery: quiet for 3 months first, steroids pre-/post-op (± oral). Trab + MMC or tube. Defer cataract ≥6 months after trab. Hypotony risk. Cyclodestruction with caution (phthisis).
chunks.hook: Uveitic glaucoma: Beta-blocker yes. Prostaglandin & Pilocarpine — Probably not.

cards.q: Why avoid prostaglandin analogues in uveitic glaucoma?
cards.a: They may worsen inflammation and cause CMO.

cards.q: Iris bombé from 360° posterior synechiae: treatment?
cards.a: Laser peripheral iridotomy (with intensive topical steroid) or surgical iridectomy.

chunks.title: Posner–Schlossman & steroid glaucoma
chunks.tldr: PSS = one eye, IOP >40 with very mild iritis and a few fine KPs, open angle, recurrent (CMV?). Steroid response: ~1 in 3 people, IOP rises in 2–4 weeks, stop steroid → IOP falls.
points: Posner–Schlossman (glaucomatocyclitic crisis): young-middle aged men, recurrent one-sided attacks (other eye 50% at times).
Mild discomfort, haloes, blur. Few cells, fine white central KPs, corneal oedema, dilated pupil, no synechiae, open angle. IOP out of proportion.
Cause: trabeculitis; CMV, H. pylori, PGE2, HLA-Bw54.
Treat: topical steroid (only while active) + aqueous suppressants ± NSAID. Follow up: some get chronic glaucoma.
Steroid-induced glaucoma: ~1/3 are responders. POAG patients usually are.
Any route (topical, periocular, intravitreal, systemic, skin, inhaled). Onset 2–4 weeks. After IVTA lasts 2–4 months; Ozurdex up to 6 months.
Risks: glaucoma/OHT, family history, high myopia, children, connective tissue disease (RA).
Treat: stop or switch to weaker (FML, rimexolone, loteprednol). ~3% stay high → drops/surgery.
chunks.hook: PSS: Pressure Skyhigh, Signs Scant.

cards.q: Unilateral IOP 50 mmHg, few fine KPs, minimal flare, open angle, recurrent?
Typical onset of steroid-induced IOP rise?

chunks.title: Lens-related glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Phacolytic = open angle, hypermature cataract leaks protein, milky aqueous/white particles. Phacomorphic = closed angle, swollen lens pushes the iris forward. Fix both: remove the lens.
points: Phacolytic: lens proteins leak through an intact capsule + protein-laden macrophages block the TM.
Painful red eye, poor vision, corneal oedema, deep AC, white floating particles, milky aqueous, pseudohypopyon. Open angle.
Not the same as phacoantigenic uveitis (capsule broken → granulomatous immune reaction).
Treat: control IOP → wash out AC → cataract extraction (fragile zonules).
Phacomorphic: intumescent lens → shallow AC, pupil block, mid-dilated pupil, dense white cataract. Other eye may have a deep AC.
Treat: like acute angle closure but no miotics (push lens forward). Hyperosmotics often needed. Laser PI/iridoplasty may help. Cataract extraction = definitive.

Lens dislocation into the AC (trauma in PXF/homocystinuria, microspherophakia) → acute pupil block. Hyperosmotics, supine + dilate to reposition, PI, then lens extraction (+ AC/iris/scleral IOL). Urgent: endothelial damage.
chunks.hook: Lytic = Leaky lens (open). Morphic = More lens (closed).

cards.q: Phacolytic glaucoma: open or closed angle?
Why avoid miotics in phacomorphic glaucoma?
cards.a: They increase iris–lens contact and shift the lens forward.

chunks.title: Traumatic: hyphaema & angle recession
chunks.tldr: Hyphaema >½ AC → 80% complications. Watch for a rebleed at day 3–5. Sickle cell: avoid CAIs, act at lower IOP. Angle recession → glaucoma in <10%, mainly if ≥3 quadrants.
points: Small hyphaema: 20% complications, 80% reach 6/18+. >½ AC: 80% complications, only 1/3 reach 6/18.
Risks: IOP >50 damages the nerve, corneal blood staining, secondary haemorrhage day 3–5 (worse).
Sickle cell: sickled cells block the TM more → higher risk even at moderate IOP.
Manage: check clotting/sickle status, stop anticoagulants (with physician), no NSAIDs, sit up (sleep too), shield, limit activity.
Drops: beta-blocker, PGA, CAI (not in sickle), topical steroid (less rebleeding), atropine for large ones. No miotics. Tranexamic acid if rebleeding.
Surgery (~5%): total hyphaema, IOP >50 for 2 days or >35 for 5 days, sickle cell, prior glaucoma, kids (amblyopia).
Angle recession: tear in the ciliary body face (iris root to scleral spur). IOP rises from TM damage. Glaucoma <10% at 10 years; unlikely if <3 quadrants.
Gonio: irregular wide ciliary body band. Yearly IOP checks. Drops often fail, SLT doesn't work, trab + antimetabolite works.
chunks.hook: Hyphaema: Sit up, Shield, Steroid, check Sickle.

cards.q: When does secondary haemorrhage typically occur after traumatic hyphaema?
Which IOP-lowering drug class to avoid in sickle cell hyphaema?
Is laser trabeculoplasty useful for angle recession glaucoma?

chunks.title: Ghost cells, ICE, tumours, ingrowth, iridoschisis
chunks.tldr: Ghost cells = khaki cells in the AC ~2 weeks after vitreous haemorrhage. ICE = middle-aged woman, one eye, 'hammered silver' endothelium (Chandler, essential iris atrophy, Cogan–Reese). Epithelial ingrowth = scalloped membrane on the back of the cornea after surgery.
points: Ghost cell glaucoma: old RBCs lose haemoglobin, become stiff khaki cells, pass through a broken hyaloid face, clog the TM. After vitreous haemorrhage in aphakes/pseudophakes. Don't mistake for uveitis. Drops → AC washout → PPV.
ICE syndrome: one eye, middle-aged woman. Abnormal endothelium spreads over angle and iris → glaucoma (50%) + corneal oedema. HSV DNA found in some.
Chandler (commonest): hammered silver endothelium, corneal oedema, mild iris changes.
Essential (progressive) iris atrophy: corectopia, iris holes (pseudopolycoria), broad PAS past Schwalbe, severe glaucoma.
Cogan–Reese (iris naevus): iris nodules / diffuse naevus (mimics melanoma).
ICE treatment: drops usually fail, trab + MMC poor long-term, tube or cyclodiode; hypertonic saline → graft. Poor prognosis.
Tumours (~5%): angle invasion/seeding (iris melanoma), melanomalytic (pigment macrophages), NVG (choroidal melanoma, retinoblastoma), forward push (ciliary body melanoma).
Epithelial ingrowth: after surgery/trauma. Persistent uveitis, grey scalloped membrane on the posterior cornea, distorted pupil. Block excision + cryo, intravitreal methotrexate, tube.
Iridoschisis: elderly, both eyes, anterior iris layer splits into fibres (inferior). Angle closure in up to 90% → laser PI.
chunks.hook: ICE: Chandler (Cornea), Essential (iris holEs), Cogan–Reese (Clumps/nodules).

cards.q: Khaki-coloured cells in the AC after vitreous haemorrhage with raised IOP?
Most common ICE variant and its endothelial appearance?
Iridoschisis is associated with which angle problem?

chunks.title: Primary congenital glaucoma
chunks.tldr: Baby with watering, photophobia, blepharospasm, big hazy corneas (>12 mm before age 1), Haab striae. Gene CYP1B1. Treatment is always surgical: goniotomy or trabeculotomy.
points: ~1 in 10,000. Boys > girls. Often both eyes (asymmetric).
Types: true congenital (40%, in utero), infantile (55%, before 3), juvenile (3–16).
Cause: trabeculodysgenesis. Mostly sporadic; ~10% AR (CYP1B1).
Classic triad: epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm.
Corneal haze (oedema), buphthalmos (big eye, blue sclera, myopia, lens subluxation), Haab striae (horizontal/curved Descemet breaks), scarring.
Cupping can reverse once IOP is controlled. C/D >0.3 or asymmetry is suspicious.
EUA: IOP first (ketamine lowers IOP least; normal 10–12), cornea diameter, disc, gonio (anterior iris insertion), refraction.

Surgery succeeds in 80–90%: goniotomy (clear cornea, incise mid-TM), trabeculotomy (hazy cornea; Harms trabeculotome; or 360° illuminated microcatheter), then trab, tube, cyclodestruction. Drops only as a bridge.
Treat amblyopia and refraction. Lifelong follow-up.
Differentials: cloudy cornea (birth trauma, rubella, MPS, CHED, sclerocornea), big cornea (megalocornea, high myopia), watering (NLDO, conjunctivitis).
chunks.hook: Tears + Light hurts + Squeezing + Big cloudy eyes → congenital glaucoma until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Classic triad of primary congenital glaucoma?
Surgery when the cornea is too cloudy for goniotomy?
Anaesthetic agent that lowers IOP least during EUA?

chunks.title: Axenfeld–Rieger & Peters anomaly
chunks.tldr: Axenfeld–Rieger: posterior embryotoxon + iris strands → iris holes/corectopia (+ teeth/face = Rieger syndrome). 50% glaucoma. Genes PITX2, FOXC1. Peters: central corneal opacity with a posterior corneal defect, 50% glaucoma.
points: Posterior embryotoxon: prominent, forward Schwalbe line. Normal in up to 15%. Also in Alagille (with disc drusen).
Axenfeld–Rieger = neural crest problem. AD, high penetrance. Genes: PITX2, FOXC1, PAX6, RIEG2.
Axenfeld anomaly: embryotoxon + iris strands to it.
Rieger anomaly: + iris stromal hypoplasia, ectropion uveae, corectopia, iris holes (looks like ICE but both eyes, young).
Rieger syndrome: + few/small teeth, flat midface, broad nasal bridge, telecanthus, redundant periumbilical skin, hypospadias.
Glaucoma ~50% (childhood/young adult), often surgical.

Peters anomaly: often both eyes. Central corneal opacity with a defect in posterior stroma/Descemet/endothelium ± iris or lens stuck to it (type I cornea only, type II + lens). Glaucoma ~50%, worse than PCG. 'Peters plus' = systemic features.
chunks.hook: Rieger = iris Rips + bad teeth. Peters = cornea Patch in the middle.

cards.q: Rieger syndrome extra-ocular features?
cards.a: Dental (hypodontia/microdontia), facial (maxillary hypoplasia, telecanthus), redundant periumbilical skin.

cards.q: Peters anomaly: what's the corneal lesion?
cards.a: Central opacity with a posterior stromal/Descemet/endothelial defect ± iris/lens adhesions.

chunks.title: Aniridia & phacomatoses
chunks.tldr: Aniridia = PAX6. Sporadic cases → WAGR → screen for Wilms tumour with abdominal ultrasound. Glaucoma 75% (late childhood). Sturge–Weber: glaucoma 30% (half before age 2).
points: AD aniridia (2/3): no systemic risk.
Sporadic (1/3): may be WAGR (Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary, Retardation) because WT1 sits next to PAX6 → ~30% Wilms risk.
Screen: abdominal US every 3 months to age 5, 6-monthly to 10, yearly to 16 (or until genetics rule out WT1).
Gillespie (1%, AR, not PAX6): ataxia, learning disability.
Signs: nystagmus, photophobia, variable iris loss (stump visible on gonio), MGD, dry eye, limbal stem cell deficiency, foveal/optic nerve hypoplasia, cataract, subluxation.
Glaucoma 75%: rudimentary iris contracts over the angle. Best: tube; cyclodiode if needed.
Also: painted/tinted CLs, lubricants, careful cataract surgery (protect limbus), stem cell grafts, treat amblyopia.

Sturge–Weber: same side as the port-wine stain. Infants: trabeculodysgenesis (goniotomy). Older: high episcleral venous pressure (episcleral haemangioma). Surgery risks choroidal effusion/suprachoroidal haemorrhage.
NF1: rare, one-sided, congenital. Plexiform lid neurofibroma, congenital ectropion uveae.
chunks.hook: Sporadic aniridia = scan the belly (Wilms).

cards.q: Which aniridia patients need Wilms tumour screening?
Glaucoma mechanism in older Sturge–Weber patients?

chunks.title: Prostaglandin analogues
chunks.tldr: First-line. ↑ uveoscleral outflow. Lower IOP 27–35%. Once at night. Side effects: red eye, long dark lashes, permanent brown iris, periocular fat loss, CMO, HSV reactivation.
points: Main action: uveoscleral outflow (some trabecular too).
Strongest drop class (27–35%). Few systemic effects.
Don't use two PGAs together (can paradoxically raise IOP).
Latanoprost: first choice, fewest side effects; 5–10% non-responders.
Travoprost: fewer non-responders; Polyquad preservative.
Bimatoprost: a bit stronger, more red eye (0.01% gentler). Sustained-release implant in trials.
Tafluprost: first preservative-free, gentle on the surface.

Ocular side effects: hyperaemia, eyelash growth/darkening, irreversible iris darkening (green-brown irises most; more pigment granules, not more melanocytes), periocular skin darkening (reversible), periorbital fat atrophy (PAP), CMO (esp. after complicated cataract surgery), uveitis, HSV keratitis.
Systemic: headache/migraine, flu-like, rash.
Latanoprostene bunod: PGA + nitric oxide donor (TM outflow). Rho-kinase inhibitors (netarsudil) → TM outflow.
chunks.hook: PGA = 'Pretty Glamorous Appearance': long lashes, dark irises.

cards.q: Mechanism of prostaglandin analogues?
Which iris colour is most likely to darken with PGAs?

chunks.title: Beta-blockers & alpha-2 agonists
chunks.tldr: Beta-blockers ↓ aqueous production (21–27%). Ask about asthma & heart block, check pulse. Not at bedtime. Brimonidine: allergy common (delayed), never under 2 years (CNS depression), no MAOIs.
points: Beta-blockers reduce production. ~10% tachyphylaxis. Less effect if already on oral beta-blocker.
Avoid at bedtime (night BP dip, aqueous already low at night).
Prefer over PGA when: one eye (cosmetic), inflammation, CMO, HSV history.

Systemic: bronchospasm (can kill asthmatics; 1 in 50 non-asthmatics get airway disease in a year), bradycardia, heart block, heart failure, hypotension/falls, Raynaud, sleep problems, depression, fatigue, libido, lipids, alopecia.
Timolol 0.25/0.5% BD (no real difference) or gel once daily.
Betaxolol: cardioselective (β1), weaker, may improve nerve blood flow, safer for lungs.
Levobunolol, carteolol (intrinsic sympathomimetic activity), metipranolol (granulomatous uveitis).
Alpha-2 agonists: ↓ production + ↑ uveoscleral, maybe neuroprotective. Cross the BBB.
Brimonidine 0.2% BD: slightly weaker than timolol. Allergic conjunctivitis (can start 18 months later), granulomatous uveitis, dry mouth, fatigue. Purite version gentler.
Apraclonidine: prevent post-laser IOP spikes, short-term bridge only (tachyphylaxis, allergy).
Contraindicated <2 years (CNS depression, apnoea). Not with MAOIs.
chunks.hook: Beta-blocker: Breathing and Beats first. Brimonidine: no Babies.

cards.q: Which beta-blocker is relatively cardioselective?
Why is brimonidine contraindicated in infants?
cards.a: Crosses the blood–brain barrier → CNS depression, hypotension, apnoea.

chunks.title: CAIs, miotics, combos & systemic drugs
chunks.tldr: Topical CAIs (dorzolamide stings + bitter taste; brinzolamide white residue). Avoid with poor endothelium. Pilocarpine for angle closure. Acetazolamide: tingling, kidney stones, low K⁺, sulfa allergy, avoid in pregnancy.
points: Topical CAIs: ↓ production. TDS alone, BD as add-on. A bit weaker than beta-blockers. Can tip corneal decompensation. Sulfa-related (cross-reaction uncommon). Topical + oral together don't add up.
Dorzolamide: stinging, bitter taste, allergic blepharoconjunctivitis.
Brinzolamide: suspension, less sting, white crust on lids.

Miotics (pilocarpine): sphincter pulls iris off the angle; ciliary muscle opens TM. Uses: angle closure, aphakic/pseudophakic. Side effects: small pupil, brow ache, myopic shift, worse cataract vision, fields look worse, RD risk. Rare systemic cholinergic effects.

Combos (all with timolol except one): Cosopt (dorzolamide), Xalacom (latanoprost), Combigan (brimonidine), DuoTrav, Ganfort, Taptiqom, Azarga (brinzolamide). Simbrinza = brimonidine + brinzolamide (no timolol).
Acetazolamide: 250 mg tabs (up to 1 g/day), SR 250 mg caps, 500 mg IV. Short-term mostly.
Acetazolamide side effects: paraesthesia, fatigue, depression, GI upset, kidney stones, hypokalaemia, Stevens–Johnson, aplastic anaemia (rare). Avoid in pregnancy (teratogenic).
Osmotics (mannitol, glycerol): short-term for very high IOP.
chunks.hook: Dorzolamide = Dreadful taste. Acetazolamide = pins and needles + stones.

cards.q: Which fixed combination has no timolol?
Name 3 systemic side effects of acetazolamide.
cards.a: Paraesthesia, kidney stones, hypokalaemia (also fatigue, depression, GI upset, rare SJS/aplastic anaemia).

chunks.title: Laser trabeculoplasty (SLT/ALT)
chunks.tldr: SLT = 532 nm Q-switched YAG hits pigmented TM cells only → IOP down ~25%. Repeatable, can be first-line. Aim for 'champagne bubbles'. Careful with heavily pigmented angles (spikes).
points: SLT: 400 µm, 3 ns, start ~0.8 mJ (0.3–1.0). Focus on the TM, ~50 shots/180°. Target: tiny bubbles.
~2/3 respond in 6 months; OHT/early glaucoma ~80% drop-free at target at 3 years. Wears off but can repeat (no thermal damage).
SLT side effects: mild iritis, PAS, IOP spike (esp. pigmented angles: PXF, PDS), rare endothelial problems, HSV, CMO.
ALT: argon, 50 µm, 0.1 s, ~700 mW at the pigmented/non-pigmented TM junction, 50 burns/180°. Thermal damage → repeat not useful. PAS, spikes, CMO, iritis.
Micropulse (MLT): no visible burn, small area.
Indications: POAG, PXF, pigmentary, OHT; first-line, poor adherence, drop intolerance, avoid polypharmacy.
Not useful: angle recession.
Pre/post: apraclonidine/brimonidine. Check IOP at 30–60 min. Continue drops.
chunks.hook: SLT = Selective, Light, Try again (repeatable).

cards.q: Why can SLT be repeated but ALT less so?
cards.a: SLT causes no thermal damage to the TM; ALT does.

cards.q: End-point reaction for SLT?

chunks.title: Laser iridotomy, iridoplasty & cyclodiode
chunks.tldr: YAG PI: pilocarpine first, outer third of the iris, 150–200 µm, ~4–5 mJ, then intensive steroid. Iridoplasty: peripheral burns pull iris away (plateau iris). Cyclodiode: kills ciliary epithelium → less aqueous.
points: PI indications: primary angle closure, secondary pupil block, (pigment dispersion).

Technique: anaesthetic, apraclonidine, pilocarpine 2%, Abraham lens. Site 11–1 o'clock (fully under the lid) or 3/9 o'clock. Half-covered by the lid edge = most glare/diplopia. Outer third (protect the lens). Use a crypt.
Power ~4–5 mJ (blue iris 2–4). >5 mJ → lens damage risk. Thick brown iris → argon pre-treatment. Success = pigment gush.
After: apraclonidine, dexamethasone intensively (q10 min ×3, hourly 6–8 h, then QID for a week). IOP check at 1–2 h.
PI complications: bleeding (50%, press the lens), IOP spike, iritis (synechiae), corneal burn, focal cataract, dysphotopsia.
Iridoplasty: 500 µm, 0.2–0.5 s, 100–400 mW, 1–2 burns per clock hour in the far periphery → iris contracts → angle opens. For plateau iris, or to break an acute attack.
Cyclodiode (TS-CPC): 810 nm, ~1500–2000 mW, 1.5–2 s, back off below the 'pop', 12–24 burns avoiding 3 and 9 o'clock. Often repeat. ECP = endoscopic version.
Cyclodiode for: blind painful eye, NVG, malignant glaucoma, scarred conjunctiva, poor surgical candidates (now also seeing eyes).
Cyclodiode risks: pain, inflammation, IOP spike, VA loss 6–13%, hypotony/phthisis, (rare) sympathetic ophthalmia.
chunks.hook: PI: fully hidden or fully exposed, never half-covered by the lid.

cards.q: Iridotomy position with the highest risk of dysphotopsia?
cards.a: Half-covered by the upper lid margin.

cards.q: Which positions are avoided in trans-scleral cyclodiode, and why?
cards.a: 3 and 9 o'clock: the long posterior ciliary neurovascular bundles.

chunks.title: Trabeculectomy & antimetabolites
chunks.tldr: Make a guarded fistula: scleral flap → sclerostomy (punch) → peripheral iridectomy → aqueous to a bleb. Add MMC (0.2 mg/ml, 2 min) or 5-FU if failure risk is high.
points: Indications: drops/laser not enough, progressing despite 'good' IOP (or poor adherence), advanced disease needing very low IOP (consider early), patient choice.

Steps: pilocarpine, bridle suture, conjunctival flap (limbus or fornix based), cautery, half-thickness scleral flap, paracentesis, enter AC, Kelly punch, peripheral iridectomy, suture flap (releasable/lysable), test flow, close conjunctiva watertight, atropine, subconj steroid/antibiotic.
Post-op: steroid + antibiotic QID 2 weeks, then steroid 8–12 weeks.
Ex-Press shunt: titanium stent instead of a punch, no PI. Less hypotony/hyphaema, same IOP. Not for PACG without cataract surgery.
Failure risks → antimetabolite: previous failed surgery, conjunctival/cataract surgery, secondary glaucoma, black ethnicity, age <65, >3 years of drops.
5-FU: blocks DNA synthesis. 50 mg/ml sponge 5 min, or post-op subconj injections. Corneal epithelial defects, leaks.
MMC: alkylating, stronger. 0.2 mg/ml × 2 min (0.4 high risk). Thin cystic blebs → hypotony, late leaks, endophthalmitis. Place sponges far back.
Bevacizumab: not better than MMC, more encapsulation.
chunks.hook: MMC = Mighty, but Makes thin blebs.

cards.q: Typical intraoperative MMC dose for trabeculectomy?
Name 3 risk factors for trabeculectomy failure.
cards.a: Previous failed surgery, secondary glaucoma (NVG, uveitic), black ethnicity, young age, long-term drops, previous conjunctival/cataract surgery.

chunks.title: Shallow AC after trab: block, leak, or malignant?
chunks.tldr: Shallow AC + low IOP → overfiltration (Seidel+ = bleb leak). Shallow + high IOP + flat bleb → pupil block (closed PI) or malignant glaucoma (patent PI, myopic shift).
points: Pupil block: high IOP, flat bleb, Seidel −, iris bombé, non-patent PI → YAG the PI site / new PI.
Overfiltration: low IOP. Big bleb + Seidel − = flap too loose. Flat bleb + Seidel + = conjunctival leak. Descemet folds, choroidal detachment.
Overfiltration treatment: watch + atropine → pressure patch, big bandage CL, Simmons shell → extra conjunctival/flap sutures, reform AC with OVD. Choroidals rarely need draining.
Malignant glaucoma (aqueous misdirection / ciliolenticular block): angle-closure eyes. Shallow AC (central too), high IOP, no bleb, Seidel −, myopic shift (near vision improves!).
Malignant treatment: atropine + phenylephrine (pull lens back), mannitol → YAG hyaloidotomy through the PI (pseudophakic: capsulotomy + hyaloid) → cyclodiode → vitrectomy (clear anterior vitreous).
Untreated flat AC → PAS, endothelial damage, cataract.
chunks.hook: Malignant glaucoma: can suddenly read without glasses (myopic shift) + flat AC + high IOP.

cards.q: Post-trab: flat AC, high IOP, patent PI, myopic shift?
First-line medical treatment of malignant glaucoma?

chunks.title: Failing blebs, leaks & blebitis
chunks.tldr: Good bleb = slightly raised, pale, microcysts. Failing = flat, vascular, or encapsulated (Tenon cyst). Late leak (MMC) → infection risk. Blebitis: white bleb, red reflex OK → hourly antibiotics. Bleb endophthalmitis → tap and inject.
points: Failure sites: extrascleral (fibrosis, encapsulation), scleral (tight sutures, scarring), internal (vitreous, blood, iris, membrane).
Rescue: digital massage, release/laser-lyse sutures (day 7–14 if IOP high, bleb flat, AC deep), needling ± 5-FU/MMC, subconj 5-FU.
Late bleb leak: thin avascular cystic bleb (MMC) → 'sweating' or hole → low IOP, hypotony maculopathy, infection.
Leak treatment: sweating → autologous blood, compression sutures, flap suture. Hole → surgical revision (excise bleb, advance conjunctiva).
Infection risks: antimetabolites, inferior bleb, leaks, blepharitis. Warn patients: red sticky eye = come now. Avoid preserved lubricants.
Bugs: H. influenzae, Strep, Staph, Gram-negatives (more virulent than post-cataract).
Blebitis: painful red sticky eye, milky white bleb, mild AC, normal red reflex. Swab (don't tap the bleb). Hourly topical (ofloxacin + cephalosporin) + oral co-amoxiclav + ciprofloxacin ≥5 days.
Bleb endophthalmitis: severe, hypopyon, vitritis, poor red reflex. Tap + intravitreal vancomycin + ceftazidime, repeat at 48 h ± PPV, oral FQ 10–14 days, steroids after 48 h. Poor prognosis.
chunks.hook: White bleb + clear vitreous = blebitis. White bleb + hazy vitreous = endophthalmitis.

cards.q: Key sign distinguishing blebitis from bleb-related endophthalmitis?
cards.a: Vitreous involvement (vitritis, impaired red reflex) = endophthalmitis.

cards.q: Encapsulated bleb is also called?

chunks.title: Non-penetrating surgery, MIGS & tubes
chunks.tldr: Deep sclerectomy/viscocanalostomy: AC not entered → less hypotony, less IOP drop. MIGS: mild–moderate glaucoma, target ~15–17, often with phaco. Tubes (Ahmed valved, Baerveldt/Molteno non-valved): for scarred, failed, or tough secondary glaucomas.
points: Deep sclerectomy: two scleral flaps, leave a thin trabeculo-Descemet window. Collagen implant, later YAG goniopuncture.
Viscocanalostomy: dilate Schlemm canal with viscoelastic, tight flap (little bleb).
Non-penetrating: POAG mainly; IOP drop less than trab, safer for advanced fields.
MIGS (no bleb): Trabectome, Kahook Dual Blade (cut TM), iStent, Hydrus (bypass TM), iTrack canaloplasty.
MIGS (bleb): Xen, PreserFlo/InnFocus microshunt + MMC (often need needling).
MIGS results: ~5–7 mmHg drop + fewer drops, but often confounded by phaco (~15% drop alone). No long-term data. Failure may make later trab harder.
Tubes: tube to AC (or sulcus/pars plana) + plate behind. Capsule forms around the plate.
Molteno (polypropylene plates), Baerveldt (big silicone plate), Ahmed (valve, must prime; less early hypotony, more encapsulation).
TVT study: tubes comparable to MMC trab. ABC study: Baerveldt lower IOP (12.7) than Ahmed (14.7) at 5 years.
Tube indications: heavy conjunctival scarring, failed trab + antimetabolite, NVG, ICE, aniridia, trauma, some congenital.

Tube complications: hypotony, encapsulation (1–6 weeks), malposition (corneal/lens touch), erosion, endothelial loss, blockage, late failure ~10%/yr, diplopia (esp. superonasal plate → acquired Brown).
chunks.hook: Ahmed = Automatic valve (less early hypotony). Baerveldt = Bigger plate, lower IOP.

cards.q: Which tube has a pressure-sensitive valve?
Nd:YAG procedure used after deep sclerectomy to boost flow?
Tube plate in the superonasal quadrant can cause?
